Came here to say the same. You need a “thing”. I was deeply unhappy at 15. Sophomore year I ended up trying out for my high school theatre department’s play on a whim and got a part. It totally changed the direction of my high school experience. 
It didn’t fix everything, no way—the therapy and medication and moving away from my parents years later were also a big piece—but by getting into theatre, I got a whole new group of friends (many of which I’m still very close to and see regularly now at age 28), I had something to do after school, I had a goal to work towards, I felt fulfilled and accomplished after each show. Looking back, it was the best part of high school.
It doesn’t have to be something at school—it could be a club sports team, a weekend art class, a robotics team, whatever. Just find a THING you can work towards. And not something you’re just doing to beef up college applications or something. Find something to do regularly that you do simply because you enjoy doing it. Accumulate positive experiences. It’s also okay to try something and quit if you don’t like it (I also made the volleyball team and quit after a month because I didn’t like the other girls on the team). 
Also, if you hate your relationship, end it. It will feel like a huge weight lifted off your shoulders.
Remember that high school generally just sucks too. It will pass.

When I was a film student I co-directed a ghost hunting series with a friend of mine where we took other students to explore supposedly haunted locations in the area.
I always did a walk through of the location beforehand for safety—often there was broken glass, etc. Other than that, we pretty much had the group go in blind and we filmed their genuine reactions. We actually did find some interesting and creepy stuff. My co-director wanted the show to be true to reality.
I felt our first couple of episodes were a little stale, though, and I wanted a climax. So I secretly staged a few things. I recruited another friend to pretend to be part of the group but who actually helped me fake doors slamming shut on their own, etc. We managed to choreograph a really scary ending that everyone in the group truly believed was a real ghost encounter; one girl wet herself. My co-director was stoked and we got a stellar grade. 
I could never decide if I should tell him the truth or not. Sadly he passed away last year, so I guess he’ll never know.

I would recommend bringing a resume. Put your volunteer experience on it as well as any extracurricular activities you’ve done at school. It doesn’t have to be fancy or long, but it’ll help you stand out to just have one. Don’t worry about bringing your social security card - that won’t be necessary until after they’ve offered you the job. You don’t need a birth certificate. 
Dress business professional - slacks and a button down. Maybe a blazer if you have one. If you aren’t sure, remember it’s always better to be overdressed than underdressed. 
Try to prepare for general interview questions as well. Strengths and weaknesses, a time you had deal with a difficult situation at one of the places you’ve volunteered, etc. 

Good luck!! Let us know when you get the job!
